summary: Ages 6–7 add and subtract two two-digit numbers (e.g. 34+27, 63−28) by giving meaning to 'carrying' and 'borrowing' as fair exchange: ten ones can be swapped for one ten and vice versa. Learners partition into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose a ten when the ones exceed nine, or decompose a ten when there are too few ones to subtract. Concrete base-ten work and pictorial jottings for the SAME calculation let the recording mirror the physical action, so regrouping is felt as a swap rather than rehearsed as a digit trick.
misconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51
Smaller-from-larger subtraction: 63−28 done as 8−3 in the ones, answer 45
Counting every unit and losing the ten-structure (not treating a ten-rod as one ten)
Misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat

activities.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
steps: Set out 34 + 27 on a place-value mat using base-ten blocks (or draggable on-screen tens and ones).

Pile the ones together to find there are eleven; because that is ten or more, perform a 'make a ten' action that swaps ten loose ones for one ten-rod moved into the tens column, leaving one loose one, then read the answer as 61 (not 511, not 51).
Set out 63 − 28; find there are not enough ones to give eight, so take a ten-rod and break it into ten loose ones, so 63 is now 50 and 13.
Hand over eight ones (13−8=5) and subtract the tens (50−20=30) to reach 35.
Record each physical step as a matching jotting: 30+20=50, 4+7=11, exchange → 61; and 63 = 50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30 → 35.
Say aloud why 34+27 cannot be 511 ('ten ones is the same as one ten, so the extra ten joins the tens').
activities.insight: Composing a ten (addition) and decomposing a ten (subtraction) are the same exchange run in opposite directions; 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are fair swaps between ones and tens, not separate digit tricks.

activities.title: Subtraction as finding a difference on a number line
steps: Place 28 and 63 on a number line.
Count up from 28 to 63 in convenient jumps (e.g. 28 → 30 is 2, 30 → 60 is 30, 60 → 63 is 3).
Compare this count-up answer with the take-away/exchange answer from the mat and confirm they agree.
Optionally model the same subtraction with a bar model (whole 63, known part 28, missing part found as the difference) or on a hundred square, as further representations of the same difference.
activities.insight: Subtraction can be read as the difference between two numbers found by counting up, which offers a second route to the same answer and a self-check against the smaller-from-larger error.

activities.title: Annotated worked example and targeted consolidation
steps: Study a worked example of 34+27 and 63−28 where the partition and exchange step are revealed one stage at a time (e.g. reveal 4+7 becoming 'one ten and one'; reveal the tens as 30+20+10).
Explain in your own words what happened at the exchange step before moving on.
Then work a short set of two-digit ± two-digit items, including 34+27 and the decomposition of 63 into 50+13, choosing or writing the answer and giving the exchange reasoning.
When a '511', '51' or '45' answer appears, say why it is wrong rather than only marking the correct one.
activities.insight: A clearly staged worked example makes the partition and exchange visible for reference, and a focused problem set surfaces whether the compose-a-ten and smaller-from-larger errors have really been overcome.

checkQuestion: Give the child base-ten blocks and paper and set two calculations to work with the blocks and record: 34 + 27, then 63 − 28. Watch what they do at the ones in each case.
checkAnswer: 61 and 35. For 34+27: 30+20=50 and 4+7=11, exchange ten ones for a ten → 61. For 63−28: too few ones, exchange a ten for ten ones (63 as 50+13), 13−8=5 and 50−20=30 → 35.
